column4: This repeats 95:6 almost verbatim: believers who do righteous deeds have أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, placing the uncut reward after the surah's scene of toil toward the Lord and judgment.
This is the same promise without an exception clause: faith and righteous action receive أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, directly confirming that the recompense is neither cut nor reduced.
God promises the Prophet أَجْرًا غَيْرَ مَمْنُونٍ; the section explicitly sets this personal promise beside the identical reward promised to faithful workers.
The people made happy receive عَطَاءً غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍ, an unsevered gift stated with a different cutting word and therefore a direct semantic counterpart to غير ممنون.

What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, and the patient are recompensed by the best of their deeds; this directly explains how a returned wage can stand outside life's dwindling line.
Every soul tastes death, yet wages are paid in full on Resurrection Day; death ends the earthly run without cutting off the recompense.
The verse joins both key nouns: those who do not follow expenditure with مَنّ or hurt have أَجْرُهُمْ عِندَ رَبِّهِمْ, a reward free of the giver's reproach.
The command not to nullify charity by الْمَنِّ وَالْأَذَى makes human reproach a cause that destroys an otherwise good deed, illuminating the opposite force of God's unburdening reward.
The Bedouins count Islam as a favor to the Prophet, but the same ayah reverses the claim: God is the one who favored them by guiding them to faith.
Joseph says قَدْ مَنَّ اللَّهُ عَلَيْنَا and immediately affirms that God does not waste the reward of those who do good; gracious divine menn and preserved recompense meet in one ayah.
Whoever performs righteous deeds as a believer fears neither injustice nor هَضْمًا, an explicit assurance that the return will not be diminished.
One who believes in the Lord fears neither بَخْسًا, shortchanging, nor رَهَقًا, an oppressive burden; both clauses clarify a reward that is unreduced and does not weigh upon its receiver.
A believer who does righteous work enters the Garden and is provided for بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ, making the return to intentional action inexhaustible rather than merely equivalent.
The patient are paid their reward بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ, another direct formulation of recompense not bounded by a diminishing measure.
Solomon is told هَذَا عَطَاؤُنَا فَامْنُنْ أَوْ أَمْسِكْ بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ; the positive bestowing sense of the named root stands beside a gift without reckoning.

Those who do good receive الْحُسْنَىٰ وَزِيَادَةٌ and are people of the Garden; this is the section's named حسن formulation in which beautiful action returns as the most beautiful outcome plus increase.
God says He does not waste the reward of whoever أَحْسَنَ عَمَلًا, explicitly moving حسن into intentional work and its preserved wage.
Believing men and women who act righteously receive a good life and a reward according to بِأَحْسَنِ مَا كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ, joining faith, work, wage, and “best.”
God removes the worst of their deeds and pays أَجْرَهُم بِأَحْسَنِ الَّذِي كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ, a direct recurrence of the best deed becoming the measure of reward.
Those who believe and do righteous deeds are promised recompense by أَحْسَنَ الَّذِي كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ, the same transfer from good work to best return.
God rewards them by the best they did, adds from His bounty, and provides without reckoning; the ayah makes the wage both “best” and more than a finite equivalence.
Every small or great expenditure and every traversed valley is recorded so that God may reward them by the best they did, making no intentional effort disappear from the return.
God created death and life to test who is أَحْسَنُ عَمَلًا; death, the section's cutter of a lifetime, is placed inside the trial of best action rather than made the end of its value.
Whoever intends the Hereafter, strives for it with its due striving, and is a believer finds that striving appreciated; intention, work, faith, and returned recognition coincide.
For one who does righteous deeds while believing, there is no denial of the striving and it is written down, directly opposing a work whose return is lost or cut.
A human being has only what he intentionally strives for, grounding the section's definition of عمل in purposeful exertion.
The striving named in 53:39 will be seen, so the deed does not vanish when its earthly performance ends.
The striving is then recompensed with the fullest recompense; this ayah supplies the returning wage completed by 53:39-40.
The Book gives believers who do righteous deeds good news of أَجْرًا حَسَنًا, joining the section's work, wage, and حسن vocabulary.
The recipients of the good reward in 18:2 remain in it forever, explicitly supplying the duration implied by “uncut.”
The people settled in the lasting abode say that no weariness touches them there; the reward cannot leave its traveler stranded through the fatigue developed in the section.
The Garden's people are touched by no fatigue and are never expelled from it, combining the negation of exhaustion with uninterrupted possession.
Paradisal fruit is لَا مَقْطُوعَةٍ وَلَا مَمْنُوعَةٍ, neither cut off nor withheld, turning the section's cutting sense into a concrete provision scene.
The promised Garden has food and shade that are دائم, a concrete image of provision whose supply and shelter do not run out.
God calls the blessed provision His رزق and says مَا لَهُ مِن نَّفَادٍ, explicitly denying depletion.
The martyrs rejoice that God does not waste the reward of believers, preserving recompense beyond their deaths.
Those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer are assured that God does not waste the reward of those who set things right.
Thirst, fatigue, hunger, each step, and every gain against an enemy are written as righteous work because God does not waste the reward of those who do good; even weariness cannot sever the return.
The command to be patient is grounded in the assurance that God does not waste the reward of those who do good.
Joseph's worldly establishment is followed by the rule that God does not waste the reward of those who do good, displaying a return already given within earthly life.
God answers that He never lets the work of any worker, male or female, be lost, directly securing intentional action against disappearance.
Patient people who do righteous deeds form the exception to the preceding human swings of despair and boastfulness, and they receive forgiveness and a great reward.
Humanity is placed in loss, matching the downward general line from which 95:6 makes its exception.
Faith and righteous action open the same exception from 103:2's universal loss, with mutual truth and patience specifying the life that escapes it.
Humanity is described as created anxiously unstable, establishing another general human condition later interrupted by an exception.
إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ breaks the general condition of 70:19 with the same exception movement that breaks the descent in 95:6.
Those within the exception affirm the Day of Recompense, directly opposing the denial questioned in 95:7 and explaining why their work can carry beyond death.
Humanity toils toward its Lord and will meet Him; the strenuous journey supplies the road on which the section contrasts fatigue that stops with reward that does not.
The person who asks only for this world has no خَلَاقٍ in the Hereafter, the named derivative's explicit picture of an absent good share opposite the uncut wage.
Those who ask for good in both worlds have a share of what they earned, completing the contrast begun in 2:200 with a returned portion tied to acquisition.
Those who trade God's covenant and their oaths for a small price have no خَلَاقَ in the Hereafter; a short worldly payment displaces the lasting share.
One who purchases magic is said to have no خَلَاقٍ in the Hereafter, another concrete use of the named root's “good share” sense as something forfeited.
The unbelievers wait for رَيْبَ الْمَنُونِ to overtake the Prophet; their hope that death will cut his life stands against God's promise of an uncut reward to him in 68:3.
The Prophet is commanded وَلَا تَمْنُن تَسْتَكْثِرُ, forbidding a gift or favor made to obtain more; his own uncut wage therefore cannot be a human favor that exacts a larger return.
The righteous feed others while wanting no recompense and no thanks from them, freeing recipients from the debt and pressure associated with reproachful giving.
God rewards those givers for patience with Garden and silk; the return comes from God after 76:9 explicitly refuses payment from the human recipient.
The Godfearing person gives wealth to purify himself, staging intentional good work without exploiting its recipient.
No one has a favor with him that must be repaid; this expressly removes the interpersonal debt carried by the section's burdensome menn.
The giving seeks only the face of the Most High Lord, locating the act's purpose beyond human repayment.
The giver will ultimately be satisfied, completing 92:18-20 with a divine return rather than a demanded human one.
God does not wrong even an atom's weight; He multiplies a good deed and grants a great reward, replacing possible diminution with increase.
A person who brings a good deed receives ten like it and no one is wronged, making the earned return enlarged rather than reduced.
People have ranks according to what they did, and God fully repays their works without wronging them, an explicit non-diminished wage for action.
Those who intend worldly life and its adornment are paid their works in full within it and are not shortchanged there, demonstrating the dictionary claim that a work's return can be worldly.
The people fully paid in 11:15 have only Fire in the Hereafter and their deeds there collapse, marking the boundary between a finite worldly return and the uncut otherworldly wage.
The one who seeks the harvest of the Hereafter receives increase in it, while the seeker of the worldly harvest receives some of it but has no share in the Hereafter.
The ayah distinguishes one who desires the reward of this world from one who desires the reward of the Hereafter, making the two domains of returned recompense explicit.
God gives the faithful both the reward of this world and the beautiful reward of the Hereafter, directly realizing the section's twofold definition of ecr.
Whoever wants worldly reward is reminded that with God are the rewards of both this world and the Hereafter, holding both returns under one divine source.
The addressed people consume their خَلَاق as earlier peoples consumed theirs and plunge into the same vain talk; an allotted share used up in the nearer life reverses the enduring good share.
When death comes, the dying person asks to be returned, identifying death as the point at which the earthly course of action is cut.
The request is to return and do righteous work, but a barrier remains until resurrection; work can no longer be resumed although its judgment and return remain ahead.
Against the source dictionary's image of a snapped rope, believers are commanded to hold fast together to حَبْلِ اللَّهِ; the held rope supplies a concrete opposite of severed continuity.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by harm, extending 2:262-264 by distinguishing a gift that leaves no wound or oppressive reminder.
The source dictionary explains memnūn through a rope being cut; this ayah literally stages extending a rope and then cutting it, though its own context concerns rage at divine aid.
Moses' companion says they have met weariness from their journey; the scene concretizes the section's dictionary explanation of fatigue stopping a traveler on the road.
This ayah supplies the abundant fruit whose supply 56:33 then declares neither cut off nor withheld.
After Joseph's earthly return in 12:56, this ayah states that the reward of the Hereafter is better for believing, mindful people.
God revives the dead and records what people sent ahead as well as the traces they left, so death does not erase the intentional work whose return awaits.
Every soul is paid in full for what it earned and no one is wronged, a general judgment-day formulation of unreduced return.
On the day each soul pleads for itself, everyone is paid in full for what they did and is not wronged.
On that day no soul is wronged and people are recompensed only for what they did, joining action to an exact return beyond death.
Every soul is paid in full for what it did, and God's complete knowledge prevents any work from being lost in the reckoning.
Creation in truth leads to each soul being recompensed for what it earned without injustice, linking created order to undiminished return.
Whoever earns a good deed receives an increase in its goodness; the حسن root here names a return that grows rather than being reduced.
Immediately before people await the Prophet's menūn in 52:30, he is told that by his Lord's favor he is neither soothsayer nor mad; divine favor sustains the one whose death they await.
By the Lord's favor the Prophet is not mad; this positive grace directly precedes his uncut wage in 68:3 and parallels the wording of 52:29-30.
God's sending of a messenger is called a favor conferred upon the believers; the positive divine subject distinguishes this menn from a human reminder that burdens its recipient.
People are reminded that God conferred favor on them after they once stood in the same condition as those they now confront, making divine menn a transforming mercy rather than a boast.
The challengers ask whether these are the people God favored among them; the ayah identifies gratitude, rather than indebted humiliation, as the fitting response to divine menn.
The messengers say that God bestows favor on whomever He wills among His servants, a direct positive use of the named root with God as giver.
God tells Moses that He had already conferred favor on him another time, locating menn in a history of rescue and care rather than reproach.
God wills to confer favor on the oppressed and make them leaders and inheritors; divine menn here lifts a burden instead of laying one on the receiver.
God says He conferred favor upon Moses and Aaron, introducing the rescue and victory that follow as beneficent menn.
The people of the Garden say God favored them and protected them from the scorching torment, joining positive menn to an otherworldly gift preserved from loss.
The Prophet says that any wage he might have asked is for the hearers themselves and that his own wage rests only with God, removing human debt from his service.
Noah asks no wage from his people and places his reward only upon God, separating prophetic work from a favor held over its recipients.
Noah says he asks his people for no wealth because his wage is only with God, a concrete stance of service without human repayment.
Hud asks no wage from his people; his reward belongs to the One who originated him, tying creation to a recompense that does not burden the addressee.
The Prophet asks no wage except that whoever wills should take a path to the Lord, turning the supposed payment into benefit for the hearer.
The townspeople are told to follow messengers who ask no wage and are rightly guided, making freedom from demanded repayment a sign of trustworthy guidance.
The Prophet asks no wage for the message and disclaims artificial pretension, keeping his work free of an obligation imposed on hearers.
Joseph's story is a reminder to the worlds for which the Prophet asks no wage, so its hearers are not made debtors to him.
The Prophet follows earlier guidance and tells his hearers that he asks no wage for it; revelation is offered as a reminder rather than a reproachful favor.
This ayah supplies the painful punishment immediately before 84:25's word-for-word exception, so the exception's rescue from the preceding outcome remains visible.
Immediately before 40:40 promises believing workers provision without reckoning, the believer contrasts this world's brief enjoyment with the Hereafter as the lasting abode.
Between the worldly-only request in 2:200 and the earned share in 2:202, these speakers ask for good in both this world and the Hereafter, completing the section's two domains of recompense.
Worldly wealth and children are adornment, while enduring righteous deeds are better with the Lord in reward and hope; passing possession, lasting work, and recompense meet explicitly.
God increases the guided in guidance, and enduring righteous deeds are better with the Lord in reward and final return, directly pairing lasting action with lasting recompense.
People prefer the nearer life, naming the choice of the perishing domain over the reward beyond it.
The Hereafter is better and more enduring, providing the explicit opposite to the preference stated in 87:16.
Worldly gifts are temporary enjoyment and adornment, whereas what is with God is better and more enduring; this is a direct passing-versus-remaining account of return.
What people receive is temporary worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more enduring for believers who trust Him.
Creation of the heavens and earth is made a test of who is best in deed, another direct movement of حسن from creation into intentional work.
Earth's adornment is a test of which people are best in deed, using the same أَحْسَنُ عَمَلًا formulation that the section connects to recompense.
God accepts the best of these believers' deeds and overlooks their evils among the people of the Garden, turning أحسن action into an accepted otherworldly outcome.
God recompenses those who do good with الْحُسْنَى, directly joining beautiful action to the most beautiful return.
The expenditure passage begins with a seed multiplying to seven hundred and beyond, so the reward beside 2:262's ban on reproach grows rather than diminishes.
After the nullified charity of 2:264, sincere expenditure is a high garden whose yield doubles and still receives dew, picturing an act whose return is preserved and increased.
Those who spend by night and day, secretly and openly, have their reward with their Lord and no fear or grief, extending the same expenditure-and-reward sequence beyond reproach.
A gift made to increase through people's wealth does not increase with God, while alms seeking God's face are multiplied; motive determines whether giving truly returns an increase.
Those excepted from human instability in 70:22 are constant in prayer, giving the exception an act characterized by continuity.
The long description of those excepted from 70:19 ends with their being honored in Gardens, supplying the lasting outcome of the exception.
One who leaves home migrating to God and His messenger, then is overtaken by death, already has his reward incumbent on God; death cuts the journey but not its intended work's return.
The blessed taste no death beyond the first death and are protected from torment, directly denying death any second power to terminate their reward.
A person within the Garden asks whether they will die, introducing the precise mortality question raised by the section's menūn image.
The answer excludes every death after the first and excludes punishment, making the rewarded life immune to the event that cuts earthly duration.
No human before the Prophet was granted earthly immortality, and his possible death will not make his opponents immortal; this sets the boundary between a mortal messenger and his uncut wage.
The opponents are asked whether the Prophet demands a wage that leaves them burdened by debt, precisely contrasting an oppressive human payment with his God-given reward.

Within the same surah that promises the Prophet an uncut wage, his opponents are asked whether his requested wage has burdened them with debt; the answer separates divine reward from human obligation.
The Prophet is asked whether he seeks payment, then told that his Lord's payment is better and that He is the best provider, locating the superior wage wholly with God.
Those who migrate after being wronged receive a good settlement in this world, while the reward of the Hereafter is greater, another explicit two-domain return.
Abraham is given his reward in this world and is among the righteous in the Hereafter, directly illustrating recompense returning in both domains.
Those killed in God's path do not have their deeds allowed to go astray, so death cannot erase the work whose result God preserves.
Those killed in God's path are alive with their Lord and provided for, supplying the post-death scene behind 3:171's assurance that believers' reward is not lost.
Whoever does an atom's weight of good sees it, making even the smallest intentional good return rather than disappear.
Whoever does an atom's weight of evil sees it, marking the exact boundary that confirms deeds of either kind survive to their return.
Even a mustard-seed weight hidden in a rock or anywhere in creation is brought forth by God, a concrete image of no deed becoming inaccessible to recompense.
The record omits neither small nor great deeds, people find what they did present, and the Lord wrongs no one; work is preserved whole for its return.
The good workers whose reward is not wasted in 18:30 receive lasting Gardens and ornaments, and the ayah calls this an excellent reward and resting place.
Believers who do righteous deeds are lodged in Garden chambers to remain there, explicitly calling that abiding destination the excellent reward of workers.
Repentant, steadfast doers receive forgiveness and Gardens in which they remain, followed by the judgment that this is an excellent reward for workers.
The Garden's inheritors settle wherever they wish and call it the excellent reward of workers, placing enduring freedom inside the work's returned wage.
The question announces the greatest losers in works, opening a precise reversal of the section's preserved wage.
Their striving goes astray in worldly life while they think they are doing beautiful work, exposing mistaken أَحْسَنَ صُنْعًا as the opposite of rewarded righteous action.
Because they deny God's signs and the meeting with Him, their works collapse and receive no weight at resurrection, a direct reversal of an unreduced wage.
Those who migrate and are then killed or die are promised good provision from God, so either form of death fails to cut the journey's return.
God admits those migrants to an entrance pleasing to them, completing the promised provision of 22:58 after their death.
Whoever comes to God as a believer having done righteous deeds receives the highest ranks, reversing the downward line through the same faith-and-work condition.
Those high ranks are Gardens beneath which rivers flow, with the recipients remaining there, supplying the unbroken duration of 20:75's reward.
Any believing man or woman who does righteous deeds enters the Garden and is not wronged even by a tiny amount, matching both the condition and the unreduced result.
Believers who perform righteous deeds are named the best of creatures, directly joining the faith-and-work exception to a transformed human standing.
Their reward with their Lord is everlasting Gardens in which they remain forever, making the return to 98:7's work explicitly unending.
Believers who do righteous deeds receive Gardens with rivers beneath, and the ayah names this the great attainment rather than a reward that can be cut short.
The Prophet is told to contrast the punishment with the Garden of Eternity, which is a reward and destination for the mindful.
The Garden's people have whatever they wish while remaining there, and the lasting gift is a promise for which God is answerable.
Believers who do righteous deeds receive the Gardens of Paradise as hospitality, restating the section's condition with its otherworldly return.
They remain there and seek no transfer away from it, making the reward in 18:107 stable and uninterrupted.
God pays the reciters and givers their wages in full and increases them from His bounty, explicitly replacing diminution with surplus.
Believers who do righteous deeds are paid their wages in full and receive an increase from divine bounty.
Believers who do righteous deeds are paid their wages in full, a direct formula of recompense without reduction.
Those who believe in God and all His messengers are promised their wages, with forgiveness and mercy locating the payment in divine grace.
The Prophet and his opponents will die; this explicit shared mortality limits earthly life while leaving the separately promised uncut wage beyond that boundary.
Noah asks his people for no wage because his wage rests only with the Lord of the worlds, freeing his hearers from human indebtedness.
Hud repeats that he asks no wage and that his wage belongs only with the Lord of the worlds.
Salih repeats the same refusal of human payment and places his wage only with the Lord of the worlds.
Lot repeats the prophetic stance of seeking no wage from his people and receiving it only from the Lord of the worlds.
Shuayb repeats the same formula, making service without a reproachful human claim a shared prophetic stance.
Charitable men and women who offer God a good loan have it multiplied and receive a noble reward, so purposeful giving returns enlarged.
The rewarded are told to enter the Garden in peace on the Day of Eternity, explicitly naming the duration into which they enter.
They have whatever they wish there and God has still more, completing 50:34 with provision that exceeds a closed measure.
